catalog_quote: There is a length distinction in the vowels and between single and geminate consonants that is phonemic and important for correct pronunciation. The following minimal pairs demonstrate length distinction for vowels: a aˈro:ha ‘compassion’ aroˈha: ‘underside of chin’; e ˈse ‘a’ ˈse: ‘not’; i ˈni ‘some’ ˈni: ‘pumice’; o ˈmano ‘ten thousand’ maˈno: ‘shark’; u ˈtaku ‘my’ taˈku: ‘adze’. These distinctions not only reflect vowel length but also affect the stress patterns, since primary word stress normally falls on the penultimate vowel and secondary stress on the one or more preceding vowels. By contrast, utterance stress creates a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels. ... [2.1.1 Phonotactics] This means that if a minimal utterance consists of a verb, it must contain four mora, or syllables, where a long vowel counts as two mora. ... [p. 8] Verbs having four or more vowels and nouns of three or more vowels may be cited in isolation, e.g. suruˈmaki ‘insert’, ha:ˈnota ‘go fishing’, taˈhito ‘base’, kereˈkere ‘earth’.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (439 PDF pages, text present; re-extracted pp. 18-19 and 34 with extracted text, no scanned). QUOTE: on p. 18 = printed p. 7 (running head 'Brief grammatical sketch 7', section 2.1 Phonology, directly under the vowel-length minimal pairs) the passage is there word for word: 'These distinctions not only reflect vowel length but also affect the stress patterns, since primary word stress normally falls on the penultimate vowel and secondary stress on the one or more preceding vowels. By contrast, utterance stress creates a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels.' The minimal pairs on the same page are exactly as reported (aˈro:ha 'compassion' / aroˈha: 'underside…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate vowel counted by morae: a long vowel counts as two (p. 7 'a long vowel counts as two mora'), so a word-final long vowel takes the stress (taˈku: 'adze' vs ˈtaku 'my'; maˈno: 'shark' vs ˈmano). Equivalent to 'stress the penultimate mora', i.e. a quantity-sensitive right-edge rule of the usual Polynesian type; vowel-length contrasts thus shift the stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on 'the one or more preceding vowels' (no explicit alternation rule for the word; at utterance level 'a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels').
new_statements.exceptions: 'normally' — no lexical exceptions listed. One- and two-syllable words are not cited in isolation: a minimal utterance needs four morae (verbs prefixed by lengthened e:, nouns take an article) (p. 7). Utterance-level stress overrides word stress. Polar questions are marked by rising pitch on the penultimate syllable and falling pitch on the final; if the final syllable is a long vowel the fall is realised on that syllable alone (p. 23).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('primary word stress'), explicitly contrasted with utterance stress. Moyle's fn. 1 (p. 7) says the phonology discussion 'draw[s] substantially on' Clark 1998 (Mele) and Donner 1987 (Sikaiana); the stress sentence is near-verbatim Donner's Sikaiana wording, but the stress-marked Takuu minimal pairs are Moyle's own data and confirm the mora-counting penult rule for Takuu.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Takuu proper (Takū/Mortlock atoll, Bougainville, PNG), i.e. taku1257 itself; no dialects distinguished. Note the provenance caveat: Moyle's stress sentence is modelled on Donner 1987 (Sikaiana, sika1261, already in our catalog with near-identical wording) per his own footnote, so the two catalog entries are not fully independent in wording, though the Takuu minimal pairs (ˈtaku vs taˈku:) are first-hand Takuu data.

tone.quote: Primary stress falls on the penultimate vocalic mora; secondary stress is placed on every second mora to the left of the stressed mora. This implies that long vowels are sequences of two identical short vowels, so that long vowels do not constitute independent phonological segments, cf. [΄mano] 'ten thousand' and [ma΄noo] 'shark, generic', [a΄rooha] 'compassion' and [aro΄ffaa] 'underside of chin', etc. Note that long and short vowels do not show differences in quality, and a long vowel is acoustically almost twice as long as its short counterpart. [...] Grammatical particles are mostly unstressed, even if they contain a long vowel.
